knowledge: Students should understand that health information encountered online may contain misinformation, misleading advertising, manipulated images, unsupported claims, or AI-generated content. title: Decision-making & personal responsibility
knowledge: Students will understand that personal health and wellness are influenced by everyday choices and that choices can have short-term and long-term consequences. Students will understand the role of personal responsibility in making health-enhancing decisions.
skills: Students will be able to apply a decision-making process to realistic health scenarios, identify possible choices and consequences, and select a responsible course of action that supports personal health and wellness.
objective: Students will analyze everyday health situations and use a decision-making process to determine responsible choices by considering options, potential consequences, and how each choice may affect their health and wellness.

criteria.text: Identify the health-related decision in a scenario.
Generate at least two possible choices.
Identify possible positive and negative consequences of each choice.
Select a responsible, health-enhancing choice.
Explain the reasoning behind their decision.

existing_check: Give students a new individual scenario:
You have had a busy week and are exhausted. You still have homework to finish, friends are messaging you to hang out online, and you have to wake up early tomorrow.
Students independently identify:
1. What decision needs to be made?
2. What are two possible choices?
3. What is one consequence of each?
4. What would you choose?
5. Why is that a responsible health decision?
Teacher circulates and checks whether students are considering consequences, rather than simply labeling choices as “good” or “bad.”
“One Choice Matters”
Students complete:
One everyday health choice I have control over is __________.
One possible consequence of that choice is __________.
Personal responsibility means __________.
Optional final discussion question:
“Does being personally responsible mean always making the perfect choice? Why or why not?”

title: Environment & health
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Individual health is influenced by personal behaviors and surrounding social and environmental conditions.
Air quality, water quality, housing, transportation, healthcare access, food access, recreation, and neighborhood safety can influence health.
Risk factors increase the likelihood of negative health outcomes, while protective factors can support health.
Community conditions can make healthy choices easier or more difficult without determining an individual's outcome.

Identify community risk and protective factors.

Recommend realistic community-level interventions and justify them with evidence.
objective: Students will analyze how environmental and community conditions influence individual and population health by evaluating community scenarios and identifying health risks, protective factors, and realistic interventions.

criteria.text: Identify at least four environmental or community factors that influence health.

title: Public health systems
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Public health focuses on protecting and improving the health of populations, while healthcare primarily treats individuals.
Local, state, and federal public-health agencies have different but overlapping roles.
Core public-health functions include surveillance, prevention, environmental health, health education, emergency preparedness, and outbreak response.
A health disparity is a measurable difference in health outcomes or opportunities; the difference alone does not prove its cause.

title: Environmental hazards & prevention

A hazard is a potential source of harm; exposure is contact with the hazard; risk is the likelihood/severity of harm under specific conditions.
Risk can depend on dose or intensity, duration, and frequency of exposure.
Common environmental health hazards include air pollution, UV radiation, excessive noise, heat, contaminated water, and chemical exposure.
People can often reduce risk through practical protective behaviors even when the hazard cannot be completely removed.

Perceived social norms can influence behavior even when those perceptions are inaccurate.

title: Addiction & the adolescent brain
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Addiction is a chronic, treatable health condition involving changes in brain circuits related to reward, stress, learning, and self-control.
Tolerance, physical dependence, and addiction are related but different concepts; physical dependence alone does not necessarily mean addiction.
The adolescent brain is still developing, including systems involved in planning, impulse control, reward, and decision-making.
Psychoactive substances can alter neurotransmission and affect judgment, coordination, mood, memory, and behavior.
Risk for substance-use problems is influenced by many factors, including age of first use, genetics, stress, mental health, family/peer influences, availability, and protective factors.
skills: (Skills)
Use credible sources to explain how substances affect the brain and behavior.
Distinguish tolerance, dependence, misuse, and addiction using accurate health terminology.
Evaluate claims about addiction and adolescent vulnerability.
Identify risk and protective factors without assuming that any single factor causes addiction.
objective: Students will use credible health information to explain how psychoactive substances affect the brain, distinguish tolerance, dependence, and addiction, and analyze why adolescence can be a period of increased vulnerability to substance-related harm.

criteria.text: Accurately distinguish tolerance, physical dependence, and addiction.
Explain at least two ways psychoactive substances can affect brain function or behavior.
Identify at least three factors that can increase or reduce substance-use risk.
Explain why adolescent brain development can affect risk-taking and decision-making.
Use a credible source to support at least one claim about addiction or the adolescent brain.

existing_check: Students individually classify short examples as tolerance, physical dependence, risky use, or possible signs of addiction and justify two answers using evidence from class.

title: Tobacco & vaping
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Nicotine is highly addictive and can affect attention, learning, mood, and impulse control, especially during adolescence.
Cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, nicotine pouches, and e-cigarettes differ in delivery method but can all create nicotine exposure.
E-cigarette aerosol is not simply water vapor and may contain nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals, and other substances.
Marketing, flavors, product design, social media, peer norms, and misconceptions can influence youth nicotine use.
Combustible tobacco remains especially harmful because burning tobacco creates many toxic chemicals, while vaping is not harmless and is not appropriate for youth.
skills: (Skills)
Analyze how advertising, social media, peers, flavors, product design, and perceived norms influence nicotine use.
Evaluate common claims about vaping using credible evidence.
Identify persuasive marketing techniques and intended audiences.

objective: Students will analyze the health effects of nicotine and tobacco products and evaluate how marketing, social norms, and misconceptions influence adolescent vaping and tobacco use.

criteria.text: Explain why nicotine can be especially concerning during adolescence.
Identify at least three health risks associated with tobacco or vaping.
Analyze at least three influences that can shape youth nicotine use.

title: Alcohol: effects, impairment, decisions
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that can impair judgment, coordination, reaction time, memory, and decision-making.
Alcohol effects depend on factors such as amount consumed, rate of consumption, body size/composition, food intake, medications, and individual variation.
Binge drinking and rapid consumption can sharply increase risk of injury, alcohol poisoning, unsafe decisions, and other harms.
Adolescents face additional risks because alcohol can impair judgment in situations involving driving, consent, conflict, and other safety decisions.
Long-term heavy alcohol use can affect multiple organ systems and increase risk for alcohol use disorder.
skills: (Skills)

Identify immediate and longer-term consequences of possible choices.

objective: Students will explain how alcohol affects the body and behavior and apply a structured decision-making process to realistic situations involving impairment, peer pressure, transportation, and safety.

criteria.text: Identify at least four short-term effects of alcohol that can affect safety or decision-making.

existing_check: Individual alcohol-related decision scenario using the class decision-making framework, including options, consequences, safest choice, and justification.
scope_focus: Short- and long-term effects; impairment; binge drinking; decision-making scenarios

title: Marijuana, prescription drugs & opioids
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Cannabis can affect attention, reaction time, coordination, memory, and judgment; effects and risks vary with dose, potency, route, frequency, and individual factors.
Prescription medications can be beneficial when used as directed, but using someone else's medication, taking more than prescribed, or using it for a different purpose is misuse.
Opioids can slow breathing; overdose can become life-threatening.
Illicitly manufactured fentanyl may be present in counterfeit pills or other illicit drugs, making appearance an unreliable indicator of contents.
Naloxone can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose, but emergency medical assistance is still needed.
skills: (Skills)
Use credible health sources to evaluate claims about marijuana, prescription drugs, opioids, and fentanyl.
Differentiate prescribed use from prescription-drug misuse.
Recognize major opioid-overdose warning signs and identify appropriate emergency actions at a high level.
Explain why counterfeit pills and unknown drug contents increase risk.
objective: Students will use credible health information to evaluate common claims about marijuana, prescription-drug misuse, opioids, and fentanyl and identify strategies that reduce overdose and misuse risk.

criteria.text: Identify at least three ways marijuana can affect functioning or safety.

title: Influences, decisions & refusal skills
knowledge: (Knowledge)
Substance-use decisions can be influenced by direct peer pressure, indirect social norms, media, family expectations, stress, availability, and perceived benefits.
Effective refusal does not require a long explanation; clear, confident communication and leaving the situation can be appropriate.
Planning transportation, allies, exits, and responses before a risk situation can make safer decisions easier.
Helping a friend does not require accepting unsafe behavior or keeping dangerous situations secret.
Bystander choices can influence whether a risky situation escalates or becomes safer.
skills: (Skills)
Identify direct and indirect pressure in realistic situations.
Demonstrate assertive verbal and nonverbal refusal strategies.
Use delay, alternative, exit, and support-seeking strategies.
Apply communication and decision-making skills to peer-pressure and bystander scenarios.
Evaluate how social norms and media can shape perceived expectations.
objective: Students will analyze peer, social, and media influences on substance-use decisions and demonstrate assertive refusal, exit, and bystander communication strategies in realistic scenarios.

criteria.text: Identify at least three influences operating in a realistic substance-use scenario.

criteria.text: Define probability, house edge, and gambler's fallacy accurately.
Solve a simple probability or expected-value problem correctly.
Explain, in your own words, why house advantage guarantees that gambling businesses profit over time.

existing_check: 3 short questions — (1) define house advantage in your own words, (2) explain the gambler's fallacy using an example, (3) a simple probability calculation (e.g., probability of rolling a specific number on a six-sided die). Circulate during the activity to observe group discussions and correct misconceptions in real time.
scope_focus: What counts as gambling; probability vs. perception; house advantage; why random systems cannot be reliably beaten
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can (1) define probability, house edge, and gambler's fallacy accurately, and (2) solve a simple probability/expected-value problem correctly on the exit ticket, with at least 4 of 5 questions correct.

title: Psychology of gambling
knowledge: Students will know the basic neuroscience of the brain's reward pathway (dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in response to rewarding or exciting experiences); how variable, unpredictable reinforcement produces a stronger and more persistent dopamine response than predictable reward, and why this is central to how gambling and other addictions take hold; the concept of tolerance (needing more risk or a bigger bet over time to get the same feeling); what a 'near miss' is and why it activates reward circuitry almost as strongly as a win; the pattern of chasing losses; and why the adolescent brain — where the limbic/reward system matures years before the prefrontal cortex responsible for impulse control and long-term judgment — is measurably more vulnerable to developing addictive patterns than the adult brain.
skills: Students will be able to explain, using accurate brain-science vocabulary, how the reward pathway and variable reinforcement drive continued gambling behavior, and identify at least one personal risk factor related to impulsivity, reward-seeking, or the timeline of adolescent brain development.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 2 (Analyzing Influences) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to describe the neuroscience of the brain's reward pathway (dopamine, the nucleus accumbens, variable reinforcement, tolerance) and explain why the mismatch between adolescent reward-seeking and impulse-control development increases vulnerability to gambling and other addictive behaviors.

criteria.text: Match key terms (dopamine/reward pathway, variable reinforcement, near miss, tolerance, chasing losses) to accurate definitions or scenarios.
Describe the mismatch between reward-system and prefrontal-cortex development in the teen brain.
Explain why that mismatch increases adolescent vulnerability to gambling and other addictive behaviors.
Identify risk factors that raise a person's vulnerability to problem gambling.
criteria.note: Original said 'name one PERSONAL risk factor in a written reflection'. Tickets never ask for personal disclosure, so this is stated generally; the reflection itself stays a classroom activity.

existing_check: Written reflection: 'Using at least three vocabulary words from today (dopamine/reward pathway, variable reinforcement, near miss, tolerance, chasing losses), explain why someone might keep gambling even while losing money, and describe why the teen brain is especially vulnerable.' Observe group discussion during the spinner activity to check understanding informally.
scope_focus: Reward systems, variable reinforcement, near misses, chasing losses, and adolescent vulnerability
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly match at least 4 of 5 key vocabulary terms (dopamine/reward pathway, variable reinforcement, near miss, tolerance, chasing losses) to accurate definitions or scenarios, accurately describe the mismatch between reward-system and prefrontal-cortex development in the teen brain, and can name one personal risk factor in a written reflection.

title: Sports betting & gambling marketing
knowledge: Students will know how sportsbooks, betting apps, and daily fantasy sports operate; common marketing tactics used to attract new bettors (sign-up bonuses, 'risk-free' bet language, streak/loyalty rewards, celebrity and influencer promotion); and how these tactics normalize betting, particularly for a younger audience.
skills: Students will be able to analyze a marketing message to identify persuasive techniques and the target audience, and begin producing a counter-message (PSA) that addresses one identified tactic.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 2 (Analyzing Influences) and Standard 8 (Advocacy)
objective: Students will be able to identify at least three persuasive marketing techniques used in sports betting advertising and explain how those techniques normalize gambling for young people.

criteria.text: Identify at least three persuasive marketing techniques used in sports-betting advertising.
Identify the intended audience of a betting advertisement.
Explain how these techniques normalize gambling for young people.
Draft a PSA message that addresses at least one of these techniques.

existing_check: Each group shares out one identified marketing technique and one early idea for their counter-message. Teacher checks worksheets for accuracy while circulating.
scope_focus: Sportsbooks, apps, advertising, promotions, influencers, fantasy sports, and normalization of betting
criteria_original: A student/group meets the objective if their marketing-analysis worksheet correctly identifies 3 or more persuasive techniques with the intended audience for each, and their group has a draft PSA message addressing at least one of those techniques by the end of class.

title: Healthy decision-making & getting help
knowledge: Students will know the warning signs of problem gambling, common financial and social consequences, the steps of a decision-making model applied to risk situations, and where to find help (school counselor, trusted adult, National Council on Problem Gambling Helpline).
skills: Students will be able to apply a decision-making model to a gambling-related risk scenario and demonstrate a refusal/communication strategy through role-play.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 5 (Decision Making) and Standard 4 (Interpersonal Communication)
objective: Students will be able to list at least three warning signs of problem gambling, apply a decision-making model to a scenario, and demonstrate at least one effective refusal statement in a role-play.

criteria.text: Identify warning signs of problem gambling.
Apply every step of a decision-making model to a risk scenario.
Use a clear refusal statement.
criteria.note: Performed/observed in class; the ticket tests the knowledge behind it.

criteria.text: Identify where to find help for problem gambling (school counselor, trusted adult, helpline).
Describe common financial and social consequences of problem gambling.

existing_check: Summative Assessment:

Administer the Unit 5 summative exam (see the accompanying Unit 5 Summative Assessment document), covering probability/house edge, psychology of gambling, marketing influence, and healthy decision-making/help resources. Allow the full block for students to complete it independently.
scope_focus: Warning signs of problem gambling, financial/social consequences, scenarios, refusal strategies, and help resources
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they list 3+ accurate warning signs on the decision-making worksheet, complete all steps of the decision-making model for the assigned scenario, and use at least one clear refusal statement during the role-play.

title: Injury risk overview
knowledge: Students will know that unintentional injuries (motor vehicle crashes, falls, drowning, and similar preventable events) are a leading cause of death and serious injury among teens; that many of these injuries are predictable and preventable rather than random 'accidents'; and how protective behaviors — wearing a seatbelt, wearing a helmet, and similar habits — measurably reduce the risk of serious injury or death.
skills: Students will be able to locate and interpret credible injury-prevention data (e.g., from the CDC or NHTSA) and use that data to evaluate their own risk behaviors.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to locate and accurately interpret real injury-prevention statistics, and explain how specific protective behaviors (seatbelts, helmets) reduce the risk of serious injury.

criteria.text: Summarize the main finding of a credible data source on teen injury risk.
Explain why protective behaviors (seatbelts, helmets) reduce the risk of serious injury.

existing_check: 'Summarize one statistic from today's data stations in your own words, and explain one protective behavior that reduces that risk.' Circulate during the station activity to check that groups are reading the data accurately.
scope_focus: Teen injury data, seatbelts, helmets, preventable injuries
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly summarize the main finding of at least one credible data source on teen injury risk, and explain in their own words why a protective behavior (seatbelt/helmet use) reduces injury risk.

title: CPR/AED Part 1: hands-only CPR
knowledge: Students will know the signs of cardiac arrest, the concept of the 'Chain of Survival' (recognize, call 911, start compressions, use an AED, hand off to EMS), and the correct technique for hands-only CPR: calling for help first, hand placement in the center of the chest, and compressing hard and fast at a steady rate until help arrives.
skills: Students will be able to demonstrate correct hand placement, compression depth, and a steady compression rate for hands-only CPR.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 7 (Self-Management) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to correctly demonstrate the steps of hands-only CPR, including recognizing when to call 911 and performing compressions with correct hand placement and rate.

criteria.text: State the first two steps of the Chain of Survival (recognize the emergency, call 911).
Demonstrate correct hand placement for hands-only CPR compressions.
criteria.note: Performed/observed in class; the ticket tests the knowledge behind it.

criteria.text: Demonstrate a steady, correct compression rate.
criteria.note: Performed/observed in class; the ticket tests the knowledge behind it.

existing_check: Skills check: each student demonstrates correct hand placement and 10–15 seconds of compressions at a steady rate while the teacher observes and gives immediate feedback. This is a practical check, not a written quiz.
scope_focus: Hands-only CPR practice
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can state the first two steps of the Chain of Survival (recognize/call 911) and demonstrate correct hand placement and a steady compression rate during guided practice, as observed by the teacher.

title: CPR/AED Part 2: AED use & organ donation
knowledge: Students will know the basic steps for using an AED (turn it on, follow its voice prompts, attach the pads as pictured, stand clear during analysis/shock, resume CPR when instructed) and how CPR and an AED work together in the Chain of Survival. Students will also know the basic facts of organ donation registration and be able to identify and correct common myths (e.g., that being a registered donor changes the medical care someone receives, or that donation prevents an open-casket funeral).
skills: Students will be able to demonstrate the basic sequence of AED use in combination with CPR, and construct an accurate advocacy message that corrects a specific organ-donation myth.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 8 (Advocacy) and Standard 7 (Self-Management)
objective: Students will be able to demonstrate the correct sequence of AED use alongside hands-only CPR, and create an accurate, persuasive message correcting a common organ-donation myth.

criteria.text: Correctly sequence the steps of AED use.
Explain how an AED and hands-only CPR work together in the Chain of Survival.
State the fact that corrects a common organ-donation myth.

existing_check: In pairs, assign each pair one organ-donation myth. Students write a short, accurate 'myth vs. fact' message (2–3 sentences) correcting it, as if creating a poster or social post. Teacher circulates to check accuracy of the corrected fact and observes the AED practice run-throughs for correct sequencing.
scope_focus: AED use; benefits and myth-busting on organ donation registration
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly sequence the steps of AED use during a practice run-through, and their myth-busting message accurately states the fact that corrects the myth they were assigned.

title: Home & School Safety (no lesson plan file yet)
scope_focus: Fire safety, basic first aid

title: Digital & road safety
knowledge: Students will know how distracted driving (texting, talking, adjusting devices, eating, managing passengers) measurably slows reaction time and increases crash risk, and will know healthy technology habits that support safety more broadly, such as not using a phone while walking near traffic, setting boundaries around notifications, and being cautious about sharing real-time location publicly.
skills: Students will be able to evaluate their own habits around phone use while driving, riding, or walking, and commit to at least one specific, personal safety change.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 7 (Self-Management) and Standard 2 (Analyzing Influences)
objective: Students will be able to explain how distraction measurably affects reaction time and safety, and identify a specific personal commitment to reduce a distraction-related risk in their own life.

criteria.text: Explain how distraction slows reaction time and raises crash risk.
Identify technology habits that support safety (e.g., no phone near traffic, notification boundaries, careful location sharing).
Distinguish specific, realistic safety commitments from vague ones.
criteria.note: Original: 'write one personal safety commitment'. Written commitment stays in class; the ticket tests what makes a commitment specific and realistic.

existing_check: Written personal commitment: 'Based on today's activity, write one specific, realistic change you will make to reduce a distraction-related risk in your own life (driving, walking, or biking).' Observe pair activity for engagement and accurate recording of results.
scope_focus: Distracted driving, safe technology habits
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can explain, using the reaction-time activity, how distraction slows response time, and write one specific, realistic personal safety commitment.

title: Synthesis: safety fair
knowledge: Students will consolidate knowledge from across the unit: injury data and protective behaviors, hands-only CPR and AED use, organ donation facts, fire and first-aid safety, and distracted driving/digital safety.
skills: Students will be able to synthesize what they've learned into a clear advocacy presentation for peers, and demonstrate at least one hands-on safety skill (hands-only CPR compressions) to a practical standard.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 8 (Advocacy) and Standard 7 (Self-Management)
objective: Students will be able to present accurate, unit-based safety information persuasively to peers, and demonstrate correct hands-only CPR technique as a practical skills check.

criteria.text: A group meets the objective if their Safety Fair booth/presentation accurately represents their assigned topic and includes at least one actionable takeaway for the audience; a student meets the CPR skills check if they demonstrate correct hand placement and a steady compression rate for 15–20 seconds without teacher correction.

existing_check: CPR Skills Check:

While Safety Fair booths are up (or immediately after), pull students individually or in small groups to demonstrate hands-only CPR: correct hand placement and a steady compression rate for 15–20 seconds, observed and checked off by the teacher. This is the unit's practical, certification-style assessment in place of a written summative test.
scope_focus: Project or certification-style assessment

title: Macronutrients & micronutrients
knowledge: Students will know the three macronutrients (carbohydrates, protein, and fat) and the general role each plays in the body; that micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) support body functions in smaller amounts; and how the MyPlate model represents a balanced, proportional approach to eating across food groups.
skills: Students will be able to locate and interpret credible nutrition information (such as MyPlate.gov) and apply it to build an example of a balanced meal.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 1 (Core Concepts) and Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information)
objective: Students will be able to identify the three macronutrients and their general roles, and use the MyPlate model to build an example of a balanced meal.

criteria.text: Name the three macronutrients and one general role of each.
Identify a balanced meal using the MyPlate model (proportions from at least four of the five food groups).
Describe the general role of micronutrients (vitamins and minerals).

existing_check: 'Name the three macronutrients and one job each does in the body. Then describe one balanced meal using the MyPlate model.' Circulate during the build-a-plate activity to check for common misconceptions in real time.
scope_focus: Core nutrition concepts; MyPlate model
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly name the three macronutrients with one role each, and their MyPlate example includes a reasonable proportion from at least four of the five food groups.

title: Nutrition labels
knowledge: Students will know the parts of a standard nutrition facts label (serving size, calories, % Daily Value, macronutrient breakdown, added sugars) and how serving size relates to portion size (the amount a person actually chooses to eat).
skills: Students will be able to accurately read and interpret a nutrition facts label to compare two food products and estimate a reasonable portion size using simple visual references.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to correctly identify the key parts of a nutrition facts label and use that information to compare two products, and estimate portion sizes using simple visual references.

criteria.text: Identify serving size, calories, and key nutrients on a nutrition facts label.
Compare two labeled products using label information.
Explain the difference between serving size and portion size.
Estimate a reasonable portion size using simple visual references.

existing_check: Worksheet check: review completed label-comparison worksheets for accuracy while circulating. Quick verbal check: ask 2–3 students to explain, in their own words, the difference between serving size and portion size.
scope_focus: Reading labels, portion sizes
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly identify serving size, calories, and at least two nutrients on a sample label, and correctly compare two labeled products using that information.

title: Physical activity guidelines
knowledge: Students will know the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) as a framework for planning physical activity, and general physical activity guidelines for teens (regular daily movement including aerobic activity, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activity several days per week).
skills: Students will be able to apply the FITT principle to describe or adjust a physical activity plan, and use a simple method (talk test or perceived effort) to monitor exercise intensity.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 7 (Self-Management) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to apply the FITT principle to plan a physical activity and use a simple method to gauge exercise intensity.

criteria.text: Define the four FITT components (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type).
Apply FITT to plan a sample physical activity.
Describe how the talk test or a perceived-effort scale shows exercise intensity.

existing_check: Review completed FITT worksheets for accurate application of all four components. Quick verbal check: ask 2–3 students to explain how they'd use the talk test to check their own intensity during a workout.
scope_focus: The FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type)
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly define all four FITT components and apply them to a sample activity, and can describe how the talk test or a perceived-effort scale indicates exercise intensity.

title: Food & fitness marketing
knowledge: Students will know common marketing techniques used on food packaging and in advertising (front-of-package health claims like 'natural' or 'low-fat' that can distract from the full nutrition label, health-halo effects) and common patterns in social-media fitness marketing (influencer-promoted products or trends, dramatic before/after claims, and unrealistic or unverified results).
skills: Students will be able to analyze a food package or a fitness-related social media post to identify the marketing technique used and evaluate the credibility of the claim being made.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 2 (Analyzing Influences) and Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information)
objective: Students will be able to identify persuasive marketing techniques in food packaging and fitness-related social media content, and evaluate the credibility of an associated health claim.

criteria.text: Identify the persuasive marketing technique used in a food-packaging or fitness social-media example.
Explain why a health claim should be checked against a credible source.

existing_check: Each group shares one identified marketing technique and their 'check the claim' response. Teacher checks worksheets for accuracy while circulating.
scope_focus: Analyzing food marketing and social-media fitness trends
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if their analysis worksheet correctly identifies the marketing technique used in at least two examples and gives a reasonable, evidence-based explanation of why the claim should be checked against a credible source.

title: Personal nutrition & activity plan
knowledge: Students will know the components of a SMART goal (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and how to apply that framework to a nutrition or physical-activity habit, along with the idea that identifying barriers and simple strategies in advance makes a goal more realistic to reach.
skills: Students will be able to write a SMART goal focused on a nutrition or physical-activity habit, and identify at least one likely barrier along with a strategy to address it.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 6 (Goal Setting) and Standard 7 (Self-Management)
objective: Students will be able to write a SMART, habit-based nutrition or physical-activity goal and identify a barrier and strategy for reaching it.

criteria.text: Identify which of the five SMART components a goal includes or is missing.
Recognize a habit-based nutrition or physical-activity goal.
Identify a realistic barrier to reaching a goal.
Match a barrier with a corresponding strategy.

existing_check: Collect (or have students self-check against a rubric) the written SMART goal and barrier/strategy plan. This is a private planning document — review for completeness of the SMART components rather than judging the specific goal chosen.
scope_focus: Students set a personal goal
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if their written goal includes all five SMART components and identifies at least one realistic barrier with a corresponding strategy.

title: Synthesis: meal & activity plan
knowledge: Students will consolidate knowledge from across the unit: macronutrients/micronutrients and the MyPlate model, reading nutrition labels, the FITT principle, evaluating food/fitness marketing, and their own SMART goal from Day 5.
skills: Students will be able to build a one-day balanced meal outline and a one-week activity outline that connect to their personal SMART goal, applying the MyPlate model and the FITT principle without relying on calorie counting or numeric food restriction.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 6 (Goal Setting) and Standard 7 (Self-Management)
objective: Students will be able to create a one-day MyPlate-based meal outline and a one-week FITT-based activity outline that support their personal SMART goal from Day 5.

criteria.text: A student meets the objective if their meal outline reflects reasonable MyPlate balance across food groups, their activity outline correctly applies all four FITT components, and both outlines visibly connect to their Day 5 goal.

existing_check: Culminating Project:

Collect the completed meal outline, activity outline, and marketing-aware note as the unit's culminating project (used in place of a written exam). Score against a simple rubric: MyPlate balance, correct FITT application, and a visible connection to the student's personal SMART goal.
scope_focus: Project or exam

title: Puberty & reproductive health basics
knowledge: Students will know the general physical and emotional changes that occur during puberty; a basic, factual overview of the male and female reproductive systems and their general functions; that the timing and pace of puberty varies widely and normally from person to person; and how to identify credible sources of information about puberty and reproductive health (a doctor, school nurse, trusted health websites such as KidsHealth or the CDC) versus unreliable sources.
skills: Students will be able to locate and evaluate credible sources of information about puberty and reproductive health, and distinguish a common myth from an accurate fact.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 1 (Core Concepts) and Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information)
objective: Students will be able to accurately describe the general physical changes of puberty and identify at least one credible source for reliable information on the topic.

criteria.text: Identify accurate facts about puberty (myth vs. fact).
Describe the general physical changes of puberty.
Name a credible source of reproductive health information.

existing_check: 'Name one physical change and one emotional change that can happen during puberty, and name one place you could go to get a reliable answer to a question about your body.' Circulate during the myth/fact activity to check understanding and correct misconceptions in the moment.
scope_focus: Grade-level appropriate, factual overview
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly identify at least 3 accurate facts on the myth-vs-fact activity and name one credible source of reproductive health information.

title: Healthy relationships
knowledge: Students will know the characteristics of healthy relationships (respect, trust, honesty, equality, support) versus unhealthy or abusive relationship patterns (control, disrespect, pressure, isolation); the definition of consent as clear, freely given, and something that can be withdrawn at any time; and the concept of personal boundaries.
skills: Students will be able to identify characteristics of healthy versus unhealthy relationships, and practice clearly and respectfully communicating a personal boundary.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 4 (Interpersonal Communication) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to distinguish healthy from unhealthy relationship characteristics and demonstrate clear, respectful communication of a personal boundary.

criteria.text: Sort relationship characteristics as healthy or unhealthy.
Explain what consent and healthy boundaries mean.
Recognize a clear, respectful way to state a boundary.
criteria.note: Original: 'state a personal boundary during role-play'. Practiced in class; ticket uses fictional scenarios only.

existing_check: Observe boundary-setting pairs for clear, respectful communication. Written check: 'List two characteristics of a healthy relationship and one sign of an unhealthy one.'
scope_focus: Respect, consent, boundaries
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly sort at least 4 of 5 relationship characteristics as healthy or unhealthy, and can state a personal boundary clearly and respectfully during the role-play practice.

title: STIs & HIV
knowledge: Students will know general, factual information about common STIs (that some are bacterial and treatable, some are viral and manageable but not curable), how STIs are transmitted in general terms as taught in standard health curricula, and prevention methods including abstinence, correct and consistent condom use, vaccination (e.g., for HPV), and regular testing. Students will know HIV-specific facts: how HIV is and is not transmitted, that HIV is a manageable chronic condition with modern treatment rather than the immediate outcome it was decades ago, and common myths that contribute to stigma (e.g., that HIV can be spread through casual contact, sharing food, or hugging — it cannot).
skills: Students will be able to locate and evaluate credible sources of information about STI and HIV prevention and testing, and correct a common myth with an accurate fact.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information) and Standard 1 (Core Concepts)
objective: Students will be able to accurately describe how STIs and HIV are and are not transmitted, identify at least two prevention methods, and correct a common HIV-related myth using an accurate fact.

criteria.text: Describe how STIs and HIV are and are not transmitted.
Identify at least two prevention methods.
Distinguish HIV myths from facts and correct a myth with an accurate fact.

existing_check: Myth vs. fact worksheet on HIV transmission (5 statements, mix of true transmission routes and common myths) completed individually, then briefly reviewed as a class. Circulate during the mini-lesson discussion to gauge understanding.
scope_focus: Transmission and prevention, with dedicated HIV segment
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can correctly identify at least two prevention methods and correctly distinguish at least 4 of 5 HIV myth-vs-fact statements.

title: Abstinence-centered decision-making
knowledge: Students will know that abstinence — choosing not to engage in sexual activity — is presented in this curriculum as the most effective method for preventing both pregnancy and STIs, because it removes the risk entirely; the steps of a decision-making model applied to a values-based, pressure-involving situation; and refusal/communication strategies for handling pressure while staying consistent with personal values.
skills: Students will be able to apply a decision-making model to a pressure-involving scenario and demonstrate a clear, respectful refusal or boundary-setting statement.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 5 (Decision Making) and Standard 7 (Self-Management)
objective: Students will be able to explain why abstinence is presented as the most effective prevention method, apply a decision-making model to a values-based scenario, and demonstrate a clear refusal statement in a role-play.

criteria.text: Explain why abstinence is presented as the most effective prevention method for pregnancy and STIs.
criteria.note: Original criterion said abstinence 'eliminates risk'; objective says 'most effective'. Using the objective's wording (HIV can also spread non-sexually). Please confirm.

criteria.text: Apply every step of a decision-making model to a values-based scenario.
Use a clear, respectful refusal statement.
criteria.note: Performed/observed in class; the ticket tests the knowledge behind it.

existing_check: Observe the decision-making worksheet and refusal role-play for each group. Written check: 'In your own words, explain why abstinence is considered 100% effective at preventing pregnancy and STIs.'
scope_focus: Abstinence presented as the most effective prevention method
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can explain in their own words why abstinence eliminates risk of pregnancy and STIs, complete all steps of the decision-making model for the assigned scenario, and use at least one clear, respectful refusal statement during the role-play.

title: Resources & advocacy
knowledge: Students will know where to access reliable information and services related to this unit's topics (a school nurse or counselor, a trusted doctor, the local health department, and established organizations such as Planned Parenthood or the CDC), general facts about the availability and confidentiality of STI/HIV testing (which varies by state and provider), and how to support a friend in accessing help without judgment.
skills: Students will be able to identify and evaluate the reliability of a health resource, and construct a respectful, accurate advocacy message encouraging someone to seek help or information.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 8 (Advocacy) and Standard 3 (Accessing Valid Information)
objective: Students will be able to identify at least two reliable resources for help or information related to this unit's topics, and create an accurate, non-judgmental advocacy message encouraging someone to use one of them.

criteria.text: Name at least two credible resources appropriate to a given scenario.
Identify where to access reliable help and testing, including confidentiality in general terms.
Identify the features of an accurate, non-judgmental advocacy message.

existing_check: Review each group's resource evaluations for accuracy and their advocacy message for tone and correctness. Quick verbal check: ask 2–3 students to name a resource they didn't know about before today.
scope_focus: Reliable resources, testing options, where to get help
criteria_original: A student meets the objective if they can name at least two credible resources appropriate to a given scenario, and their advocacy message is accurate and non-judgmental in tone.

title: Synthesis
knowledge: Students will consolidate knowledge from across the unit: puberty and reproductive health basics, healthy relationships and consent, STI/HIV facts, abstinence-centered decision-making, and reliable resources and advocacy.
skills: Students will be able to reflect on and apply the unit's decision-making and communication skills to a values-based scenario without disclosing personal information.
Aligned to National Health Education Standard 5 (Decision Making) and Standard 8 (Advocacy)
objective: Students will be able to demonstrate unit-wide understanding by applying decision-making, communication, and resource-finding skills to a values-based scenario in a reflective project.

criteria.text: A student meets the objective if their reflective project accurately applies at least three of the unit's five topics to the scenario and reflects sound, values-consistent decision-making reasoning.

existing_check: Culminating Reflective Project:

Collect the completed reflective project as the unit's culminating assessment in place of a written exam. Score against a simple rubric: accurate application of relationship/consent concepts, correct use of the decision-making model, an accurate health fact, and a credible resource recommendation with reasoning.
scope_focus: Reflective assessment or project
